analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal student aid to for-profit colleges that rely on veterans' and military tuition money.
analysis.headline: The bill had 27 Senate cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law (the '90/10 rule') says for-profit colleges must get at least 10% of their revenue from somewhere other than federal student aid, or they lose that aid. The bill would close a loophole: colleges could no longer count GI Bill benefits and military tuition assistance toward that 10%, since veterans' education benefits are federal money too. Colleges that got too much of their income from federal programs — including the ones aimed at service members and veterans — would lose eligibility for those programs for at least two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and veterans who use GI Bill benefits or military tuition assistance for college. The bill targets for-profit colleges that rely heavily on military and veteran education money, which were repeatedly found to recruit service members aggressively while delivering poor outcomes. If a college broke the revenue rule, Defense and Veterans Affairs would cut off its education programs and post the school's name on public websites so beneficiaries would know before enrolling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members and veterans using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: Redefines the 90/10 revenue limit so that GI Bill benefits, military tuition assistance, and other federal education money for service members and veterans count as federal revenue, closing the loophole that let for-profit colleges use them toward the 10% non-federal share [S2][S3].

Makes a for-profit college that misses the revenue limit two years in a row ineligible for all federal education assistance — including Defense and Veterans Affairs programs — for at least two years, and requires a two-year compliance record to get back in [S3].

Requires the Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs to cut off aid to ineligible schools and publish each school's name, the violation, and how long it is barred on public websites, so service members and veterans can see it before enrolling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit (proprietary) colleges, especially those whose business model depends on recruiting service members and veterans. Schools near the 10% revenue line would have to raise non-federal revenue, enroll fewer students paid for with federal benefits, or leave federal education programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges relying on military tuition money

drawbacks.text: The two-year penalty and two-year readmission requirement could leave enrolled students stranded mid-program if their school loses eligibility abruptly, and supporters of the schools argued the rule measures revenue mix rather than educational quality.

Because many veterans use benefits at for-profit colleges that offer online and flexible programs suited to military schedules, some schools losing eligibility could reduce options available to those students even when their programs were legitimate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct protection for service members and veterans is real: the loophole the bill closed meant a college could be 90% federally funded with taxpayer money routed through veterans' benefits and still qualify. The honest cost is on the students' side — schools that lose eligibility mid-enrollment could strand students, and the bill relied on an abrupt cutoff rather than a gradual phase-down. Weighing the two, the protection of GI Bill and military tuition dollars from schools that depend on them for revenue is the larger effect, and public notification of violations softens the surprise somewhat.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, which never held a vote on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Carper introduced the bill on June 24, 2015, with 26 Democratic and one Independent cosponsor [S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; that referral was the bill's final action [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and neither the Senate nor the House ever voted on it during the 114th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that rely on veterans' and military tuition assistance, which kept counting those federal benefits toward the 10% non-federal revenue requirement. Those benefits still counted toward the requirement under existing law after the bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges that take veterans' benefits

for.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close the 90/10 loophole for military and veteran education money.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 24, 2015 and never acted on it; no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against expanding the 90/10 rule to count veterans' benefits, a position the industry publicly defended because its schools depend on federal education revenue, including GI Bill and military tuition assistance.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents — 26 of 44 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 2 Independents — and no Senate Republican signed on; the committee with jurisdiction, then chaired by a Republican, never took it up.

industries.note: The bill would make GI Bill and military tuition money count as federal revenue under the 90/10 rule, cutting off all federal education aid — including veterans' benefits — to schools that fail the limit two years running. These schools' interest in the bill runs against service members and veterans because revenue from their benefits is what kept schools inside the law while recruiting them.
